video_title: Anthropic Goes Public as AI Stocks Crack
gist: Notable Capital's Jeff Richards defends Anthropic's IPO (priced $83, ~10x forward revenue vs 20x+ comps) as a demand-side proof point for AI while Dan Nathan flags the day-one fade, $900B compute commitments and a cracking Nasdaq/SaaS tape; CME's Terry Duffy then warns it is '2007 for retail', attacks perpetuals and prediction markets, and sees AI over-investment and long-end Treasury risk.

themes.theme: Anthropic IPO: pricing, S-1 and enterprise thesis

insights.claim: Notable Capital invested in Anthropic's Series E at a $60 billion valuation when it was an $800 million run-rate business, betting that enterprise would be the premier AI use case while consensus saw OpenAI as the leader.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Early VC thesis (enterprise > consumer) has been validated; enterprise-heavy AI exposure is the bull framing for ANT.

insights.claim: Anthropic was priced at $83 a share, roughly 10x forward revenue, versus public comps like Cloudflare, Palantir and CrowdStrike trading at 20x+ forward revenue, so Richards argues it is hard to call overvalued and the institutional order book was very strong.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Relative-valuation case: ANT at ~10x forward sales vs high-growth software comps in the 20s leaves room for multiple expansion if it executes.
insights.quote: it didn't go out at a hot money hot company bubbleicious premium that it can then try trade down from

insights.claim: Anthropic's stock priced at $83, opened above $100, hit about $115, then faded to around $97 near the close on day one, on volume near the roughly one billion shares sold, implying a valuation around $1.25 trillion.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Day-one fade from $115 to $97 signals muted demand above the deal price; watch whether $83 holds as support.

insights.claim: Richards says first-day IPO trading reflects thin, short-money flows with almost zero signal on long-term appetite, and fair value is usually found three to six months out as lockups expire and institutions add.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Don't over-read ANT's day-one action; the 3-6 month window around lockup expiries is when price discovery matters.
insights.quote: what an IPO does on the first day is largely reflective of a very thinly traded short money trade

insights.claim: About 315 million Anthropic shares were eligible to be sold by insiders and investors at IPO, with most insiders locked up and a staggered lockup expiration expected over the next six months; 20% of the deal was set aside for retail.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Staggered lockup expiries over six months create supply overhangs to trade around.

insights.claim: Anthropic's S-1 disclosed 11,000 customers spending $100,000+ a year, yet it captures less than 1% of those customers' software and technology spend, and Fortune 500 adoption is still at the pilot stage.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Low wallet share at large customers implies long runway for revenue growth into 2027-28.
insights.quote: they are less than 1% of the software and technology spend outside of those customers

insights.claim: Richards argues that with a typical 6-9 month enterprise sales cycle, the Q1 launches of Claude Code and Claude Cowork are only now converting into adoption, giving Anthropic a large tailwind into 2027-2028.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Expect enterprise AI revenue acceleration to show in coming quarters as Q1 pilots convert.

insights.claim: Pre-S-1 bear arguments that Anthropic had no gross margins, was burning cash, and was IPO-ing to raise money were dispelled by the filing, which showed strong margins, good cash flow and about $100 billion on the balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: The bear debate has shifted from unit economics to compute commitments; margin-based shorts lost their footing.
insights.quote: Oh, they have a hundred billion dollars on their balance sheet

insights.claim: Dan Nathan flags Anthropic's roughly $900 billion of compute commitments over about five years against a revenue run rate that went from about $16 billion a year ago to an expected $60 billion, and notes sequential revenue growth decelerated a little into the IPO.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Compute commitments vs revenue is the key bear metric; watch sequential growth in first public quarters.

insights.claim: Nathan warns that the moment one frontier lab pulls back from a compute commitment, for example to a neocloud, the AI trade is 'done for a bit'.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Any frontier-lab commitment cancellation is a key tail risk for neoclouds, Nvidia and AI infrastructure names.
insights.quote: The moment that one of these frontier labs pulls back from one of these commitments, whether it be to a neoccloud or something like that, the whole thing is done for a bit.

insights.claim: Richards argues Anthropic is not an 'Atlas holding up the world' but sits inside an ecosystem of thousands of partners, citing Salesforce's 'Claude Force' launch as the first domino of many large enterprises partnering with it.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Partner channel (e.g., Salesforce) extends Anthropic's distribution; track enterprise partnership announcements.

insights.claim: Richards says Anthropic's ability to IPO in a choppy, declining, risk-off market is itself a strong signal, since fundamentals-focused investors saw a genuinely good business rather than a hype-driven bubble IPO.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Demand for a quality AI IPO in a down tape suggests institutional appetite for AI with real financials remains.

themes.theme: AI ecosystem signals from private markets

insights.claim: Richards says growth rates across AI infrastructure companies (Vercel, Databricks, Supabase, Fireworks, Baseten) all accelerated in Q1 after Claude Code launched and have continued since.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Private AI-infra growth is a leading indicator for public infra and data names; watch for their IPOs.

insights.claim: Coding is the first breakout AI use case: SpaceX bought Cursor and Cognition is a private company valued at $48 billion.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: AI coding tools command large valuations; a signal for dev-tool and code-agent exposure.

insights.claim: Richards says that during Q1's 'SaaS apocalypse', private-market data on agent-driven infrastructure demand showed not all software would lose, and names like Snowflake, CrowdStrike and Palo Alto roughly doubled from those lows.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Private-market usage data front-runs public earnings; indiscriminate software selloffs create buying opportunities in infra/security/data.
insights.quote: not all software is created equal

insights.claim: Richards wants more AI ecosystem companies to go public in 2027 so public investors get more demand-side data points beyond Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Expect an AI-infrastructure IPO pipeline in 2027.

insights.claim: Citing Ben Bajarin of Creative Strategies, Richards argues AI adoption has a far larger installed base than prior cycles: about 200 million internet users in 2000 versus 8 billion people and billions of smartphone users today, many already using Gemini or ChatGPT.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Larger addressable base supports faster consumer adoption curves than the dot-com or cloud eras.

insights.claim: Richards argues the public market has only had visibility into AI's supply side (chips, hyperscalers, trillion-dollar capex), and Anthropic is the first public window into the demand side that will consume that compute.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: ANT's results become the key demand-side read-through for the whole AI capex complex.

themes.theme: AI trade cracking: Nvidia, Nasdaq and risk-off tape

insights.claim: The Nasdaq 100 is down about 15% from its recent high, which Nathan says was set around the week of the SpaceX IPO; on the Anthropic trading day QQQ gapped up 2% (about 20 times in five years) and reversed to close down 2%.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: A gap-up reversal on a marquee IPO day is a classic distribution signal; watch for follow-through.

insights.claim: Nathan suggests the AI trade can be bookended by the SpaceX IPO at the top and the Anthropic IPO day, arguing there are bear markets going on beneath the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Mega-IPOs as sentiment top markers; be cautious adding AI beta here.
insights.quote: the ground has been moving below the AI trades feet for months and months now and it really does feel like there's there are bare markets going on

insights.claim: Richards notes SCHD (holding Coca-Cola, Chevron, Target, Home Depot) is up 34% this year while QQQ is up 7%, and many AI names have fallen 30-40% over three to six months, showing a risk-off market.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Defensive/dividend rotation has dominated; potential mean-reversion setup for AI names in 2027 if they deliver.

insights.claim: Richards says Nvidia trades at about 10-12x forward earnings while Walmart trades at 40x, showing the market lacks confidence in Nvidia's outlook; if Nvidia and Anthropic deliver, the market should reward them.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Nvidia at a low multiple vs Walmart sets up asymmetric upside if AI demand holds.

insights.claim: Nathan reads Walmart's 25% straight-line rally off 52-week/multi-year lows as a bearish signal for the broader market rather than a bullish one.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Leadership by defensive mega-caps signals risk aversion.

insights.claim: Richards describes investors as being in 'cognitive overload' after 90 days of the Iran war, Nvidia news, inflation, a VIX around 27-28 and a new Democratic Congress, and expects continued volatility.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Elevated VIX and macro overload argue for smaller sizing and hedging into year-end.

themes.theme: SaaS repricing in the prompt era

insights.claim: Salesforce closed down 10% in one session, has fallen about 20% in a week without an uptick, and is 30% off post-earnings highs set after its Claude Force announcement.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Even AI-partnered incumbents are not immune; SaaS sentiment remains fragile.

insights.claim: Richards frames the existential question for traditional SaaS as what happens if users simply log into a prompt such as Claude, OpenAI or Google, pushing investors toward clear winners like CrowdStrike and Palo Alto and to question everything else.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Favor software with momentum and clear AI-era moats; be skeptical of seat-based app SaaS.
insights.quote: if the future is people logging into a prompt and that prompt is claude or something from OpenAI or Google what does that mean for enterprise software

insights.claim: Richards believes data platforms Databricks and Snowflake are big winners in the AI trend, while key open questions for software are what remain true systems of record and whether vertical or regulatory-compliance moats hold.
insights.speaker: Jeff Richards (Notable Capital)
insights.so_what: Data layer exposure (Snowflake) is preferred within software; stock picking over basket buying.

themes.theme: CME vs prediction markets and perpetuals

insights.claim: Terry Duffy argues perpetual futures are legally swaps, not futures, because the funding rate is two parties exchanging payments, and expects CME to prevail in court.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: A swap ruling would upend perps venues' registration and tax status; regulatory risk for crypto/retail derivative platforms.
insights.quote: the definition of a swap is two parties exchanging a payment to each other. And that's what that's how the funding rate works for perpetuals.

insights.claim: If perpetuals are deemed swaps, Duffy warns retail traders could lose Section 1256 tax treatment (60% long-term/40% short-term) and face ordinary income taxes, plus platforms would be out of compliance on swap registration.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Hidden tax/regulatory liabilities for retail perps users and venues.

insights.claim: Duffy says about 90% of Kalshi's prediction business is sports, that there is no money and a lot of risk in it, and that regulatory pushback is going to get 'real aggressive'.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Sports event contracts face regulatory headwinds; risk to prediction-market-dependent revenue at Robinhood/Kalshi.

insights.claim: Duffy criticizes the CFTC for allowing about 5,000 self-certified contracts, mostly prediction markets, without a single objection, many listed the next day.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Lax self-certification is a likely target for regulatory tightening.

insights.claim: Duffy says Kalshi is reportedly raising at a $64-65 billion valuation based on compute futures, even though CME filed first for compute futures with Silicon Data and was stalled when the Commerce Department cited national security.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Compute futures are an emerging contested market; watch regulatory approval as a catalyst for CME.

insights.claim: Nathan notes Kalshi's reported valuation exceeds Robinhood's market cap, yet a Kalshi executive said market-related contracts are only about 5% of revenue, making it essentially a sports trading app while DraftKings and Flutter trade at multi-year lows.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Private prediction-market valuations look stretched against public sports-betting comps.

insights.claim: Duffy says CME's portfolio margining frees up $105 billion of efficiencies daily and it moves $9-15 billion a day between buyers and sellers, a scale competitors cannot replicate without comparable liquidity and open interest.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Clearing-house network effects are CME's moat against new derivative entrants.
insights.quote: Nobody can replicate what we can do.

insights.claim: CME stock is back at all-time highs and the business grew about 15% year over year in Q3, after fears over prediction-market and perpetual competitors; Duffy says CME is up 3,700% since he took it public in 2002.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: CME has proven resilient to disruption fears; diversified volume growth in volatile markets.

insights.claim: Duffy calls the Google Cloud deal struck during the pandemic, in which Google paid CME $1 billion, a source of optionality, now extended with options to 2038-39, and argues any new exchange would be cloud-based.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Cloud migration lowers CME's tech-cost burden and is a long-dated strategic option.

insights.claim: Duffy says it feels like 2007 for retail: retail has bought every dip since March 2009, is now 'all in' and concentrated in a handful of names, creating complacency and crowded trades.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Crowded retail positioning raises downside-cascade risk; keep dry powder.

insights.claim: Nathan notes that for the first time Robinhood's event-contract volume in Q3 exceeded crypto and equities in dollar terms, a sign of elevated retail risk-taking.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Gamified retail speculation is a late-cycle signal.

insights.claim: Retail-linked stocks have collapsed: Coinbase hit multi-year lows with Bitcoin at $63-64K from $82K, and Robinhood fell from about $117 to $60-70, losing roughly $50 billion of market cap, which Duffy reads as weakening retail sentiment.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Retail brokers are a real-time read on retail health; their weakness flags retail exhaustion.

insights.claim: Duffy warns retail buying mega-IPOs without room to add on the next leg down is a concern, and says leverage products with auto-liquidation and auto-deleveraging can easily hurt them.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: IPO-chasing retail could amplify downside if mega-IPOs break issue price.

insights.claim: Duffy says roughly 70% of US trades are high-frequency or algorithmic, which can cause cascading moves on small information, so CME uses circuit breakers.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Algorithmic dominance raises flash-move risk; use limit orders and expect gap risk.

themes.theme: Bonds, banks and AI systemic-risk contagion

insights.claim: Duffy thinks Treasury yields are too low ('rates are cheap'), bonds are probably going lower and long-end yields will keep rising, citing $41 trillion of debt heading to $50 trillion and a $2 trillion deficit.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Bearish duration; favor short-end or steepener positioning.
insights.quote: I think the rates are cheap.

insights.claim: Duffy attributes 10-15 basis-point intraday swings in 10-year Treasuries to a shift from foreign to domestically dominated ownership, with hedge funds and prop shops trading on headlines.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Expect continued Treasury volatility; supports rates-hedging demand (CME volumes).

insights.claim: Duffy sees banks in good shape given their multiples and post-SVB lessons on duration risk, and is more worried about companies 'potentially too big to fail' trading at massive multiples, raising whether Nvidia is too big to fail.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Systemic risk has migrated from banks to richly valued AI mega-caps.

insights.claim: Duffy believes far more money is chasing AI than the product and adoption deployed can support, likens it to crypto, and says if it tips over there must be a trickle-out effect similar to 2008.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: AI capex overbuild risk could spread through credit; watch capex-dependent names.
insights.quote: There's way too many dollars chasing very little output of product

insights.claim: Nathan argues the roughly $1.5 trillion hyperscaler AI capex since late 2022 is increasingly financed off-balance sheet via private credit funded by banks, so a protracted Nvidia problem could become systemic; he cites Amazon selling data centers, likely to Blackstone.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Monitor private-credit/PE stocks and data-center sale-leasebacks as contagion indicators.

insights.claim: Duffy says institutions avoid DeFi because there is no know-your-client process and on-chain positions are exposed and can be front-run by algorithmic traders, which is why DeFi remains retail-dominated.
insights.speaker: Terry Duffy (CME Group CEO)
insights.so_what: Limited institutional DeFi uptake weighs on crypto-infrastructure names.
